beats.text: Which is bigger: three quarters or one half? Let’s build the amounts and find out.
beats.note: Always compare the same-sized whole.

beats.text: A fraction starts with equal parts. Here, one whole is divided into four equal pieces.
beats.note: Each piece is one quarter.

beats.text: Shade three pieces. The numerator, three, counts the shaded parts. The denominator, four, counts the equal parts in the whole.
beats.note: Numerator: parts chosen. Denominator: equal parts in one whole.

beats.text: A strip shows the same amount. Three of four equal lengths are shaded. The picture changes, but the value stays the same.
beats.note: Area models and strips show the same fraction.

beats.text: When denominators match, the pieces have the same size. Three quarters is greater than two quarters because three pieces are more than two.
beats.note: Compare the numerators when denominators match.

beats.text: Now compare one third and one sixth. These wholes are the same length, but the sixths are smaller pieces.
beats.note: More equal pieces in a whole means smaller pieces.

beats.text: So one third is greater than one sixth. A bigger denominator does not always mean a bigger fraction.
beats.note: For unit fractions, compare the size of one piece.

beats.text: Return to three quarters and one half. Split each half into two equal pieces. One half becomes two quarters.
beats.note: Renaming keeps the amount unchanged.

beats.text: Now the parts match. Three quarters is greater than two quarters, so three quarters is greater than one half.
beats.note: Same whole. Same-sized parts. Clear comparison.

beats.text: A number line shows fraction size as distance from zero. Divide the distance from zero to one into four equal intervals.
beats.note: Count intervals, not tick marks.

beats.text: One quarter is one interval from zero. One half is two intervals, and three quarters is three intervals.
beats.note: Numbers get larger as you move to the right.

beats.text: Read from left to right to order them from smallest to largest: one quarter, one half, then three quarters.
beats.note: Left to right: smallest to largest.

beats.text: Try this: which is greater, five eighths or three eighths? You can pause the video and explain your choice.
beats.note: What stays the same? What changes?

beats.text: Five eighths is greater. Both use eighth-sized parts, and five parts are more than three. Compare equal wholes, use models, and check the number line.
beats.note: Equal wholes → equal-sized parts → compare or order.

beats.text: Can one half and four eighths be the same amount? Watch the shaded length as we change the pieces.
beats.note: Equivalent means equal in value.

beats.text: Start with one half. Split every part of the whole into two equal pieces. The shaded half now contains two quarters.
beats.note: The whole and shaded amount stay the same.

beats.text: Split every quarter in half again. Now four of eight equal pieces are shaded. One half, two quarters and four eighths are equivalent.
beats.note: Smaller pieces, more pieces, same amount.

beats.text: The number rule matches the picture. Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.
beats.note: Multiplying by four over four is multiplying by one.

beats.text: For three fifths, multiply both numbers by four. Three times four is twelve, and five times four is twenty.
beats.note: Both numbers change by the same factor.

beats.text: Equivalent fractions also land at the same point on a number line. They are different names for one number.
beats.note: One half, two quarters and four eighths meet here.

beats.text: Simplifying works in reverse. Group equal pieces together instead of splitting them into smaller pieces.
beats.note: Look for a common factor.

beats.text: Group the eighths in pairs. Six eighths becomes three quarters. We divided the numerator and denominator by two.
beats.note: Three and four have no common factor greater than one.

beats.text: Try twelve eighteenths. Both twelve and eighteen divide by six. Twelve divided by six is two; eighteen divided by six is three.
beats.note: Two thirds is in simplest form.

beats.text: Be careful: adding the same number to both numbers does not preserve the value. One half and two thirds are different amounts.
beats.note: Use multiplication or division, not addition.

beats.text: We can also partition a fraction. Three quarters is three one-quarter pieces added together.
beats.note: Partitioning keeps the total amount unchanged.

beats.text: Two quarters make one half, so three quarters is also one half plus one quarter. Different partitions can describe the same amount.
beats.note: One amount can be split in different ways.

beats.text: Your turn: three fifths equals how many twentieths? Pause if you want to work it out.
beats.note: Five times which number makes twenty?

beats.text: The answer is twelve twentieths. Multiply both numbers by four. Remember: change the name, keep the value.
beats.note: Multiply or divide BOTH numbers by the same non-zero number.

beats.text: What happens when we have more than one whole? Let’s count eleven quarter-sized pieces.
beats.note: Every whole is the same size.

beats.text: Four quarters make one whole. Another four quarters make a second whole. Three quarters are left over.
beats.note: Eleven quarters makes two wholes and three quarters.

beats.text: Eleven quarters is an improper fraction. Its numerator is at least as large as its denominator. It can describe one whole or more.
beats.note: Improper does not mean incorrect.

beats.text: Two and three quarters is a mixed number. It combines two whole units with a fractional part.
beats.note: Keep a clear space between the whole number and fraction.

beats.text: To convert, divide eleven by four. Eleven divided by four is two with a remainder of three.
beats.note: The quotient counts whole units. The remainder counts quarter-pieces.

beats.text: The denominator stays four because our pieces are still quarters. So eleven quarters equals two and three quarters.
beats.note: Two complete wholes, then three more quarter-steps.

beats.text: Now go the other way. Take three and two fifths. Each whole contains five fifths.
beats.note: Three wholes contain fifteen fifths.

beats.text: Three times five gives fifteen fifths. Add the extra two fifths to make seventeen fifths.

rows.label: Three whole units, then two more fifths

beats.note: Fifteen fifths + two fifths = seventeen fifths.

beats.text: So three and two fifths equals seventeen fifths. Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator.
beats.note: Wholes × parts per whole + extra parts.

beats.text: A fraction can also equal an exact whole. Eight quarters is two wholes, with no fractional part left over.
beats.note: A zero remainder means no fractional part remains.

beats.text: To compare mixed numbers, compare the wholes first. Three and one quarter is greater than two and three quarters.
beats.note: Three wholes already exceeds two and three quarters.

beats.text: If the wholes match, compare the fractional parts. Two and one half is greater than two and one quarter.
beats.note: Both have two wholes. One half is greater than one quarter.

beats.text: Your turn: change nine quarters into a mixed number. How many groups of four can you make?
beats.note: Pause and explain the whole units and the leftover part.

beats.text: Nine quarters is two and one quarter. Two groups of four use eight quarters, leaving one quarter. Both forms name the same number.
beats.chapter: Two ways to name an amount
beats.note: Group to make wholes. Count pieces to go back.

beats.text: A half plus a quarter: do we get two sixths? No. We need equal-sized parts before we can combine them.
beats.note: Use the same whole and the same-sized parts.

beats.text: First, use matching denominators. Two sevenths plus three sevenths makes five sevenths.
beats.note: Count the parts. Keep the size of each part.

beats.text: We add the numerators and keep the denominator. We are still counting sevenths, not fourteenths.
beats.note: Never add the denominators.

beats.text: For one half plus one quarter, the denominators are related: four is a multiple of two. Rename the half as two quarters.
beats.note: Split each half into two equal pieces.

beats.text: Now add two quarters and one quarter. The result is three quarters.
beats.note: One half + one quarter = three quarters.

beats.text: Subtraction follows the same idea. For three quarters minus one eighth, rename three quarters as six eighths.
beats.note: Eight is a multiple of four.

beats.text: Take away one eighth. Five eighths remain. The denominator stays eight.
beats.note: Six eighths − one eighth = five eighths.

beats.text: On a number line, begin at six eighths and move back one eighth. You land on five eighths.
beats.note: Add: move right. Subtract: move left.

beats.text: Simplify when you can. One sixth plus three sixths is four sixths, which equals two thirds.
beats.note: Divide the numerator and denominator by two.

beats.text: Mixed numbers can make another whole. One and four fifths plus two fifths is one and six fifths.
beats.note: Six fifths is one whole and one fifth.

beats.text: Regroup five fifths as one whole. The answer is two and one fifth.
beats.note: Check: the result is a little more than two.

beats.text: For several fractions, rename them with a common denominator. One half plus one quarter minus one eighth becomes four eighths plus two eighths minus one eighth.
beats.note: A common denominator of eight works for all three.

beats.text: Four plus two minus one is five, so the result is five eighths.
beats.note: Keep the denominator eight throughout.

beats.text: Here is an extension: when neither denominator is a multiple of the other, shared multiples can help. Try one quarter plus one sixth.
beats.note: The least common multiple is also called the lowest common multiple.

beats.text: Multiples of four include four, eight, twelve. Multiples of six include six, twelve, eighteen. Twelve is the smallest positive shared multiple.
beats.note: LCM of four and six = twelve. This is extension work.

beats.text: One quarter is three twelfths. One sixth is two twelfths. Add to get five twelfths.
beats.note: Any common denominator works; the least keeps numbers smaller.

beats.text: Your turn: two thirds minus one sixth. Rename two thirds as four sixths, then subtract one sixth.
beats.note: Pause and simplify your answer.

beats.text: Three sixths remain, which is one half. Use equal wholes, rename into equal parts, calculate, and simplify.
beats.note: Same whole → rename → calculate → simplify.

beats.text: Mia mixes half a cup of oats with a quarter of a cup of nuts. How much does she use altogether?
beats.note: Both measurements use the same one-cup unit.

beats.text: First identify the whole: one cup. Altogether tells us to combine the amounts, so choose addition.
beats.note: Understand the situation; do not rely on a keyword alone.

beats.text: Rename one half as two quarters. Two quarters plus one quarter makes three quarters.
beats.note: The parts must be the same size.

beats.text: Mia uses three quarters of a cup altogether. That is more than half a cup and less than one cup, so the answer makes sense.
beats.note: State the unit, then check the size of the result.

beats.text: Now a ribbon is two metres long. We cut off three quarters of a metre. How much ribbon remains?
beats.note: One whole unit is one metre, not the entire two-metre ribbon.

beats.text: We want what remains, so subtract. Two metres equals eight quarter-metres.
beats.note: Two equal metre-lengths make eight quarter-metres.

beats.text: Eight quarters minus three quarters is five quarters. Five quarters is one and one quarter.
beats.note: Five quarters = one whole and one quarter.

beats.text: One and one quarter metres remain. On the number line, move back three quarter-steps from two.
beats.note: The remaining length must be less than two metres.

beats.text: For a comparison, Ava walks three quarters of a kilometre. Leo walks five eighths of a kilometre. Who walks farther, and by how much?
beats.note: Use the same one-kilometre unit for both distances.

beats.text: Rename three quarters as six eighths. Ava walks farther because six eighths is greater than five eighths.
beats.note: First answer who, then find the difference.

beats.text: Subtract five eighths from six eighths. Ava walks one eighth of a kilometre farther.
beats.note: The difference measures the gap between the distances.

beats.text: Here is a two-step problem. A jug holds one litre. We pour out a quarter of a litre, then another half a litre. How much remains?
beats.note: Both poured amounts are measured in litres.

beats.text: A quarter plus a half is three quarters of a litre poured out. Subtract three quarters from one whole litre.
beats.note: Three quarters poured out; one quarter stays in the jug.

beats.text: One quarter of a litre remains. Check: three quarters poured out plus one quarter remaining makes one whole litre.
beats.note: An inverse check helps catch mistakes.

beats.text: Your turn: Sam says two thirds plus one sixth equals three ninths. Explain why that cannot be right.
beats.note: Adding a positive amount must make two thirds larger.

beats.text: Rename two thirds as four sixths. Add one sixth to get five sixths. Identify the whole, model the relationship, calculate, and check your answer in context.
beats.note: Understand → model → calculate → answer with units → check.
